chunks: What the Shaykh, may Allah the Exalted support him, informed me of: from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from his father, from Saʿd ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad, from ʿUthmān ibn ʿĪsā, from Ibn Udhaynah, from Bukayr and Zurārah, the two sons of Aʿyan: that they asked Abā Jaʿfar عليه السلام about the wudu (ablution) of the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم, so he called for a basin or a vessel in which there was

water. So he washed his two palms, then dipped his right hand into the vessel and washed his face with it, using his left hand with his palm to assist in washing his face. Then he dipped his right hand into the water and scooped with it from the water, and washed his right hand from the elbow to the fingers, not returning the water to the two elbows. Then he dipped his right hand into the water and scooped with it from the water, and poured it over his left hand from the elbow to the palm, not returning the water to the elbow, as he had done with the right. Then he wiped his head and his feet up to the ankles with the remaining wetness of his two palms, and he did not renew water.
If it is said: How can you hold to that, while the apparent meaning of His saying, Exalted is He, indicates the opposite of it? For He, Exalted is He, said in the verse of wudu (ablution):
"Then wash your faces and your hands up to the elbows."

And "ilā" gives the meaning of termination and limit. Do you not see that they say, "I went out from al-Kufah to al-Baṣrah," meaning: until I reached al-Baṣrah? This would require that the elbow be the limit in wudu (ablution), not that one begin from it. It is said to him: There is nothing in the verse that contradicts what we have mentioned, because "ilā" may be in the sense of limit, and it may be in the sense of "with"; it has broad usage, and its use in that sense is evident among the people of language. He, Exalted is He, said:
"And do not consume their wealth with your wealth."
And He, Exalted is He, said, relating from ʿĪsā عليه السلام:

That is, with Allah. And it is said: So-and-so governed al-Kufah to al-Baṣrah, and the limit is not intended; rather the meaning in it is with al-Baṣrah. And they say: So-and-so did such-and-such and undertook such-and-such, this in addition to what he did of such-and-such, meaning: with what he did. And Imruʾ al-Qays said: "He has a croup like a dune made firm by dew, with a withers like a plated gate." He meant: with a withers. And al-Nābighah al-Jaʿdī said: "And the broad expanse of two forearms in a shoulder, with a breastbone that made the shoulder broad." Meaning: with a breastbone. And this is more abundant than to require elaboration in it. When it is established that "ilā" may mean "with," it indicates the obligation of washing the elbows also, according to what the discussion has entailed, and it confirms that "ilā" in the verse is not in the sense of limit.

key_terms.إِلَى: a preposition discussed linguistically as meaning either 'up to' or 'with' in context
key_terms.الْكَعْبَيْنِ: the ankles, the limit mentioned for wiping the feet
key_terms.الْمَرَافِقِ: the elbows, mentioned in the Qur'anic wording of the wudu (ablution) verse
key_terms.الْمِرْفَقِ: the elbow, identified as part of the required washing in wudu (ablution)
key_terms.الْوُضُوءِ: wudu (ablution), the ritual purification being described and discussed
key_terms.بِفَضْلِ كَفَّيْهِ: with the remaining moisture of his two palms, indicating no new water was taken for wiping
key_terms.مَسَحَ: he wiped, referring to wiping the head and feet in wudu (ablution)

ai.seo_question: How does this hadith explain washing the arms in wudu (ablution) from the elbows and the meaning of "إِلَى الْمَرَافِقِ" in the Qur'an?
ai.summary: This passage describes the wudu (ablution) of the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم as transmitted from Abā Jaʿfar عليه السلام, including washing the arms from the elbows downward and wiping the head and feet with the remaining moisture of the hands. It then presents a linguistic argument on the Qur'anic phrase "إِلَى الْمَرَافِقِ," explaining that "إِلَى" can mean not only "up to" but also "with," thereby supporting the inclusion of the elbows in washing without implying that washing must begin from the fingers.
